components.note: Picture of a double-leaf door or gate, with two posts and the swinging panels; the simplified form is a streamlined version of 門.

example.fact: 门 is also the measure word for school subjects and courses (一门课, 'one course') and for cannons, which surprises learners who know it only as 'door'. It forms many compounds for entrances, like 大门 (main gate) and 门口 (doorway).

components.note: 宀 (roof) gives the idea of a settled place under cover, which matches the sense of being fixed or stable.
疋 (foot) suggests a foot coming to rest, so the whole character reads as 'come to rest, settle'.

example.english: We have settled on a time.
example.fact: 定 often works as a resultative or fixed-in-place idea: 定下来 means to settle down or be decided, and 定 can book things in the sense of 'fix' a room or seat (定位子). Do not confuse it with 订 (dìng, to order or book), which is the usual character for reservations.

components.note: Drawn as 二 with a hooked vertical stroke through it; the shape is old and its original picture is uncertain, so treat it as a simple unit to remember.

example.fact: 于 is a formal, written preposition that covers 'in', 'at', 'to', 'from' and even 'than' depending on the verb, so it shows up in set patterns like 生于 (born in), 关于 (about) and 对于 (regarding). Everyday speech usually prefers 在, 到 or 比 instead.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) hints at a hollow tube, the original sense of the word.
官 (guān) supplies the sound; guān and guǎn differ only in tone.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì nǐ bié guǎn.
example.english: Don't get involved in this matter.
example.fact: 管 also means 'pipe or tube', and the sense of 'to manage' grew from it. A very common phrase is 不管 ('no matter, regardless'), and 管 on its own can mean 'to meddle in' or 'to take responsibility for', as in 别管我 ('leave me alone').

components.note: 攵 (a hand holding a stick) conveys forceful action, in line with acting boldly.
耳 (ear) is part of the traditional shape; its link to the meaning of daring is not clear, so treat it as a visual part.

example.pinyin: Nǐ gǎn yí gè rén qù ma?
example.english: Do you dare to go alone?
example.fact: 敢 is a modal verb placed directly before the verb, as in 敢说 (dare to say). It also appears in the polite stock phrase 我不敢当 ('I don't deserve such praise'), which is used to deflect compliments.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks the body part.
觜 (zuǐ, 'beak') gives the sound exactly and also suggests the pointed shape of a beak.

example.fact: 嘴 is the colloquial word for the mouth (as a body part for speaking and eating), whereas 口 is more formal or used in compounds like 人口 and 出口. Idioms like 嘴甜 (sweet-talking) and 多嘴 (to speak out of turn) use it for the way someone talks.

components.note: 足 (foot) shows that jumping is done with the legs and feet.
兆 (zhào) gives a loose hint of the sound; the vowel is the same but the initial has shifted.

example.english: The children are jumping on the grass.
example.fact: 跳 is used for many bouncing or sudden movements: 跳舞 (dance), 跳高 (high jump), and 心跳 (heartbeat, literally 'heart jump'). It can also describe skipping a step, as in 跳过 ('skip over').

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action is done with the hand.
爪 (claw) adds the idea of clawing or gripping, and it also echoes the sound zhuǎ.

example.fact: 抓 means to grasp with the hand or to arrest, and it has extended meanings like 抓紧 (to make the most of, hurry up) and 抓住机会 (seize the opportunity). It is more forceful and physical than 拿 (to take, hold).

components.note: 力 (strength) shows that movement takes effort.
云 (yún) appears on the left; the sound link is loose here because simplification replaced the original sound part of 動.

example.pinyin: Bié dòng, wǒ gěi nǐ pāi zhāng zhào.
example.english: Don't move, I'll take a photo of you.
example.fact: 动 is a verb on its own (别动 'don't move') and a very productive component: 运动 (sport), 动物 (animal), 感动 (to be moved), 动手 (to start doing). It also works as a result complement meaning 'able to move', as in 搬不动 ('can't move it').

components.note: 贝 (shell, an old form of money) fits the idea of profit and winning.

example.fact: 赢 is the opposite of 输 (shū, to lose). It takes a thing won or an opponent: 赢了比赛 (won the match) or 赢了他 (beat him), and learners should not confuse it with 胜 (shèng, victory), which is more formal.

components.note: Picture of a person kneeling with arms crossed, an old stylised image of a woman.

example.pinyin: Zhè wèi nǚshì shì wǒ de lǎoshī.
example.fact: 女 is mostly a bound form in modern Chinese: you say 女人 (woman) or 女孩 (girl) rather than 女 alone. It is also a very common radical in characters about women and family relationships, such as 妈, 姐 and 好.

components.note: 忄 (heart) reflects the anxious, rushed state of mind.
亡 (wáng) gives a rough sound hint, as both end in -ang.

example.fact: 忙 is an adjective, so it takes 很 rather than a verb 'to be': 我很忙. It also works as a verb, as in 忙着做饭 (busy cooking), and in the reply 'nǐ zài máng shénme?' ('what are you busy with?'), a casual way to ask what someone has been up to.

components.note: 阝 (a mound, the left-hand side form of 阜) hints at a place or fortification where people stand together.
人 (person) shows a group of people in a line or unit.

example.fact: 队 is used in 排队 (to line up, queue), 足球队 (football team), and 队长 (team captain). In everyday speech it is a collective noun and rarely takes the measure word 个, though 一个队 is acceptable.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action is done with the hand.
立 (lì) gives a rough sound hint; the finals are similar.

example.english: He is pulling me by the hand.
example.fact: 拉 is the opposite of 推 (tuī, to push), and the sign on a door says 拉 for 'pull'. It extends to 拉琴 (play a bowed instrument), 拉肚子 (to have diarrhea) and 拉近 (to bring closer), so context matters.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick) represents active effort, as in an act of help.
求 (qiú) gives the sound and also the sense of asking for help.

example.fact: 救 is the standard verb for rescuing from danger: 救命 ('help!', literally 'save life'), 急救 (first aid) and 救护车 (ambulance). It is stronger than 帮 (bāng, to help) and implies someone was in real trouble.

components.note: 目 (eye) refers to the eyes closing in sleep.
垂 (chuí) gives a rough sound hint and also the idea of drooping eyelids.

example.english: I want to go to bed earlier.
example.fact: 睡 usually appears in 睡觉 (to sleep), where 觉 is a separate noun, so the verb can be split as 睡了一觉 ('slept a sleep'). It can also be a result complement: 睡着 (to fall asleep) and 睡醒 (to wake up).

components.note: 日 (sun) points to a time of day.
免 (miǎn) gives a loose sound hint; the finals are similar.

example.fact: 晚 means 'late' as an adjective (来晚了, 'arrived late') and 'evening' as a noun, as in 晚上 and 晚饭 (dinner). Greetings use it too: 晚安 ('good night') and 晚上好 ('good evening') are common.

components.note: 门 (door) is the enclosing part and gives the sense of something shut.
才 (talent, here in its role as a bar-like shape) fits across the doorway as a latch.

example.fact: 闭 is more literary than 关 (guān): you 关门 (close a door) but 闭眼 or 闭嘴 (shut one's mouth) for body parts. It also appears in 闭幕 (close a ceremony) and 开闭 (open and close).

components.note: 土 (earth) hints at a heap of earth or a crumbling ruin.
不 (bù) is the shape on the right; the sound match is loose.

example.fact: 坏 means 'bad' for people and things, 'broken' for objects (坏了) and 'spoiled' for food. It is also used as a result complement to show something has been ruined: 玩坏 (broke through playing), 吃坏肚子 (to get a stomach ache from food).

components.note: 爫 (a hand from above) shows something being handed over.
冖 (a cover) represents the item being passed.
又 (a hand) shows the receiver's hand taking it.

example.pinyin: Tā shòu le hěn duō kǔ.
example.fact: 受 often appears in set phrases: 受伤 (to be hurt), 受欢迎 (to be popular), 受不了 (cannot stand). It can be used both for receiving good things (受到表扬, 'receive praise') and for suffering bad ones.

components.note: 辶 (movement) suggests travelling along a route.
车 (cart) shows vehicles linked together in sequence.

example.pinyin: Tā lián fàn dōu méi chī.
example.fact: The 连…都/也 pattern means 'even…': 连我都知道 ('even I know'). 连 also means 'to connect' (连接) and 'continuously' (连续), and it appears in names of cities and chains such as 连锁 (chain store).

components.note: 入 (to enter) shows something put in.
玉 (jade) is the valued item stored inside, so the whole character suggests something kept complete and intact.

example.pinyin: Quán jiā rén dōu zài kàn diànshì.
example.english: The whole family is watching TV.
example.fact: 全 can be an adjective ('whole', 全世界), an adverb ('completely', 全懂了) and a verb-like word ('complete', 齐全). A classic grammar point is that 全 modifies the noun directly, whereas 都 comes before the verb.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action of pushing something upright.
廷 (tíng) gives the sound; the final is nearly identical.

example.fact: As an adverb, 挺 means 'quite' or 'pretty' and is colloquial and mild, often followed by 的: 挺好的 ('pretty good'). As a verb it means 'to straighten up' or 'to endure', as in 挺住 ('hold on!').

components.note: 匕 (a standing figure) is the visual form of a person at a place.
止 (zhǐ) gives a loose sound hint.

example.pinyin: Cǐ rén shì wǒ de péngyou.
example.fact: 此 is the formal or written counterpart of 这, found in set phrases like 因此 (therefore), 此外 (besides), 如此 (like this) and 此时 (at this moment). It is rarely used alone in speech.

components.note: Picture of flowing water, with a central stream and drops to either side.

example.fact: 水 is one of the oldest radicals, written as 氵 on the left of characters for liquids and rivers. It also appears in everyday words like 水果 (fruit), 水平 (level, standard) and in the common saying 一水之隔 ('separated by a river').

components.note: 木 (wood) reflects that early cups were made of wood.
不 (bù) provides a loose sound clue; in older Chinese the sound was closer to bēi.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi chá.
example.english: Please give me a cup of tea.
example.fact: 杯 works as both a noun (杯子, a cup) and a measure word for drinks: 一杯水, 两杯咖啡. It also appears in 干杯 ('cheers', literally 'dry the cup'), which is said before drinking together at a meal.

components.note: 买 (to buy) is the base of the character, since selling is the opposite of buying.
十 (ten) sits on top as the extra mark that sets 卖 apart from 买.

example.fact: 卖 is the counterpart of 买 (mǎi, to buy) and differs only by the tone and the extra stroke on top. A famous tone pair is 买 mǎi vs. 卖 mài. It extends to 卖力 (to work hard) and 出卖 (to betray).

components.note: 亻 (person) shows that the word concerns people.
言 (speech) means words, so 'a person's word' is something you trust.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gěi māma xiěle yì fēng xìn.
example.english: I wrote a letter to my mother.
example.fact: 信 has two common uses: 'letter' (measure word 封) and 'to believe', as in 我不信 ('I don't believe it'). It also forms 信息 (information), 短信 (text message) and 自信 (self-confidence).

components.note: 舛 (two feet in opposition) shows the footwork of dancing.
無 (wú) is the traditional form of 无 and gives the sound; wú and wǔ differ by tone.

example.fact: 舞 is a verb and noun, but in modern speech it nearly always appears with 跳 in 跳舞 ('to dance'). Common compounds include 舞会 (ball, dance party) and 芭蕾舞 (ballet).

components.note: Drawing of a tall building or tower with a roof, a base and a gate, giving the idea of height.

example.fact: 高 covers 'tall' for people and buildings, 'high' for levels and prices, and is also a common surname. Its opposite is 矮 (ǎi, short) for people but 低 (dī, low) for levels.

components.note: 讠 (speech) reflects the idea of testing by asking or trying things out.
式 (shì) gives the sound exactly.

example.english: You can give it a try.
example.fact: 试 is often doubled or followed by 一下 for a soft suggestion: 试试 or 试一下. It is the verb for trying on clothes (试衣服) and appears in 考试 (exam) and 试用 (trial use).

components.note: 羊 (sheep) is a classic sign of something good and desirable.
大 (big or a person with outstretched arms) completes the shape of someone well-fed or imposing.

example.english: The scenery here is very beautiful.
example.fact: 美 is also the short name for America (美国) in Chinese, and it forms 美丽, 美味 (delicious), 美好 (wonderful). It is a more literary or formal word for 'beautiful' than 漂亮, which is typical for describing people.

components.note: Simplified from 書, which shows a hand holding a brush writing; the modern shape is greatly reduced and does not break down into clear parts.

example.fact: 书 takes the measure word 本 (一本书). It also appears in 书包 (school bag), 书店 (bookstore), 图书馆 (library) and in 读书, which can mean either 'to read' or 'to study'.

components.note: 王 (here the jade radical 玉) hints at a round, polished gem.
求 (qiú) gives the sound exactly.

example.fact: 球 is both a ball and a sport in compound words such as 足球 (football/soccer), 篮球 (basketball) and 地球 (the Earth). The verb pairs with the sport: 踢球 (kick), 打球 (hit or play), 投球 (throw).

components.note: Built from 木 (tree) over 旦 (dawn); the parts do not clearly explain the sense of 'check', so it is best learned as a whole.

example.fact: 查 covers checking and looking something up: 查字典 (look up in a dictionary), 查电话 (look up a number) and 检查 (inspect). In 调查 (to survey) it means to investigate, and the surname Zhā uses the same character with a different reading.

components.note: 心 (heart) shows that forgetting happens in the mind.
亡 (wáng) gives the sound and also the sense of 'lost', so the heart has 'lost' the memory.

example.english: Don't forget to bring an umbrella.
example.fact: 忘 is often paired with 了 to make 忘了 ('forgot'), and 别忘了 is the common way to say 'don't forget to'. It also appears in the set phrase 忘记 and in 难忘 ('unforgettable').

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action of striking with the hand.
白 (bái) gives a rough sound hint; the initial b/p is related.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒmen pāi zhāng zhào.
example.english: Please take a photo of us.
example.fact: 拍 literally means to pat or clap with a flat hand (拍手, to clap), but it is now the verb for taking photos (拍照) and for filming (拍电影). It also forms 拍卖 (auction) and 球拍 (racket).

components.note: 足 (foot) marks something walked on.
各 (gè) gives a rough sound hint; the finals are close in old Chinese.

example.fact: 路 uses the measure word 条 (一条路) and extends to routes and ways: 路线 (route), 路上 (on the way), 一路平安 (have a safe trip), and bus numbers (3路). 路 can also be an abstract path or method, as in 出路 (way out).

components.note: 口 (mouth) sits on top and is a visual part, with no clear tie to the meaning.
木 (tree) below suggests standing still like a tree, which fits the sense of a blank, motionless look.

example.pinyin: Bié fādāi le, kuài zuò zuòyè ba.
example.english: Stop spacing out and do your homework.
example.fact: 呆 appears mostly in 发呆 (to stare blankly, zone out) and 呆板 (stiff, wooden). In the sense 'to stay' it is read dāi and is also written 待 in the north (呆在家里, 'stay at home'); 书呆子 is a bookworm.

components.note: 囗 (enclosure) is the outer frame.
儿 (legs) forms the inner strokes; the shape is traditionally an image of four items divided.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu sì kǒu rén.
example.english: There are four people in my family.
example.fact: 四 sounds close to 死 (sǐ, death), so many Chinese people avoid it in phone numbers, floor numbers and gifts. In Chinese buildings the fourth floor is often skipped, similar to the 13th floor in the West.

components.note: Built from a person-like stroke with a stroke added, in an old picture of someone braced or supported; its exact origin is debated, so it is best learned as a whole.

example.fact: 久 describes how long something lasts, usually after 很 or in 好久 ('a very long time'). It is also in the greeting 好久不见 ('long time no see') and in 久违, a more formal way to greet someone you have not seen for a while.

components.note: 戈 (dagger-axe) shows a weapon guarding a territory.
口 (mouth or settlement) marks a place that is guarded; the original sense was a defended area, later borrowed for 'or'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē chá huò kāfēi?
example.english: Would you like tea or coffee?
example.fact: 或 and 还是 both mean 'or', but 或 is used in statements (茶或咖啡都可以) while 还是 is used in questions (茶还是咖啡？). 或 also appears in 或者 (or) and 或许 (perhaps).

components.note: 忄 (heart or mind) shows understanding as a mental act.
董 (dǒng) gives the sound exactly.

example.pinyin: Nǐ dǒng wǒ de yìsi ma?
example.english: Do you understand what I mean?
example.fact: 懂 is often used with 不 or 得 as a complement: 听不懂 (can't understand by listening), 看懂了 (understood by reading). It is stronger than 知道 (to know a fact) and means to really grasp something.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) recalls bamboo slips laid out in order.
弟 (dì) gives the sound exactly.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dì yī cì lái zhèlǐ.
example.english: This is my first time here.
example.fact: 第 is placed before a number to make it ordinal: 第一 (first), 第二天 (the second day). Unlike English, you put 第 directly before the number and then a measure word: 第三个 (the third one).

components.note: Picture of a horse in profile with a mane and legs, flattened into a few strokes in the simplified form.

example.pinyin: Nà pǐ mǎ pǎo de hěn kuài.
example.fact: 马 takes the measure word 匹. Horses appear in many idioms: 马上 (immediately, 'on horseback'), 马马虎虎 (so-so) and 一马当先 (take the lead). It is also a very common surname and in names like 马来西亚.

components.note: 讠 (speech) shows that the word is about speaking.
井 (jǐng) gives a loose sound hint; the simplified form kept this part.

example.english: The teacher is telling a story.
example.fact: 讲 is more formal and deliberate than 说: it fits lectures, stories and explanations (讲课, 讲道理). It also means 'to be particular about', as in 讲卫生 (to care about hygiene) and 讲究.

components.note: 贝 (shell, an old form of money) fits the idea of people paid for a job.
口 (mouth or opening) sits on top; here it is best seen as part of the visual shape.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen gōngsī de yuángōng.
example.english: He is an employee of our company.
example.fact: 员 is a bound form used as a suffix for people with a role: 演员 (actor), 服务员 (waiter), 运动员 (athlete), 公务员 (civil servant). It is almost never used alone.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks a spoken sound or interjection.
屋 (wū) gives a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 喔 is an interjection that signals sudden understanding or mild surprise, and it is common in Taiwan and in text messages. In mainland Chinese it is often written as 哦, and the tone can vary (ò, ó) depending on emotion.

excludeSuggestion: A spoken interjection, usually written 哦 on the mainland; the study value is low.

components.note: Drawn as a horizontal stroke over 尢; this simplified shape is a reduced form of 無, and its parts do not carry a clear meaning.

example.english: He has no home to return to.
example.fact: 无 is a literary 'no' or 'without', as in 无法 (unable to), 无聊 (boring), 无论 (no matter) and the idiom 无家可归. It is the simplified form of 無, and it corresponds to colloquial 没有 and 不.

components.note: Shape resembles a coiled form with the end tucked in; the picture is uncertain, so it is best learned as a whole.

example.fact: 已 is a written form of 'already' and is mostly seen in 已经 (already), 已 as 'to stop' in literary phrases like 不得已 (have no choice), and 而已 ('that's all'). Do not confuse it with 己 (jǐ, self) and 巳 (sì).
